The word jade has two distinct meanings as a noun. One is common and widely used today; the other is old and rarely used outside of literature.

This is the primary and most important meaning. Jade is a hard, smooth, semi-precious stone that is highly valued for its beauty and has been treasured by humans for thousands of years.

What it looks like

Jade is most famous for its rich green color — think of a deep, cool, slightly waxy-looking green. This particular shade is so associated with jade that there is a color named after it: jade green. However, jade is not always green. It also comes in white, pale lavender, yellow, orange, brown, grey, and even black. The green variety is simply the most prized and well-known.

The surface of a polished jade stone has a distinctive quality — it looks almost glassy or waxy, smooth to the touch, and has a quiet, deep luster rather than a sharp sparkle. It doesn't shine like a diamond; it glows softly.

Two types of jade

Here is something important that many learners don't know: the word "jade" actually covers two completely different minerals — nephrite and jadeite. They look similar, but they are chemically and structurally different stones. Both are called jade.

  • Jadeite is rarer, harder, and generally more valuable. Its colors tend to be more vivid and vibrant. The most prized form is an intense, almost electric green called Imperial jade — it is extremely expensive, sometimes worth more than diamonds of equivalent size.
  • Nephrite is more common and slightly softer, though still very hard. Its green tends to be deeper and more muted — olive green, dark spinach green, or creamy white. Most jade you encounter in everyday life is nephrite.

Both are genuine jade. Neither is "fake."

Why jade is special

Jade is not just a pretty stone — it carries enormous cultural and symbolic weight, especially in East Asian civilisations.

In Chinese culture, jade holds a status unlike any other material. It has been revered for over 7,000 years, far longer than even gold or silver. The Chinese consider jade to be the most noble of all stones. It is associated with virtue, purity, grace, and moral integrity. Ancient Chinese philosophers compared the qualities of a gentleman to the qualities of jade — its hardness to courage, its smoothness to wisdom, its translucence to honesty. Jade was used in royal ceremonies, buried with emperors, carved into objects of worship, and given as the most meaningful of gifts. Even today, it is extremely common to see Chinese people wearing a jade bracelet or pendant, often gifted by a grandmother or parent, believed to bring protection and good fortune.

In Mesoamerican civilisations — among the Maya and the Aztec — jade was valued even above gold. It was the color of water and crops, symbolising life, fertility, and royal power. Only rulers and high priests wore jade.

The Māori people of New Zealand carve a local form of jade (called pounamu or greenstone) into heirloom carvings that are passed down through generations and hold deep spiritual significance.

What jade is used for

Jade is used in several ways:

  • Jewellery — bracelets, rings, pendants, earrings, and beads. A jade bangle (a smooth, circular bracelet) is one of the most iconic uses.
  • Carvings and sculptures — jade is carved into animals, figures, dragons, Buddha statues, decorative bowls, and vases. The carving of jade is considered a high art form, particularly in China.
  • Ornamental objects — decorative items for homes and altars.
  • Cosmetic tools — jade rollers and gua sha stones, used in skincare for facial massage, have become globally popular in recent years.

Hardness and durability

One reason jade has been so valued throughout history — apart from its beauty — is its toughness. Jade is remarkably difficult to break or chip. It is not the hardest mineral (diamonds are harder), but it is extremely tough, meaning it resists fracturing exceptionally well. This made it useful for tools and weapons in ancient times, before metal was widely available, and it means that jade objects can last for millennia without cracking.

This meaning is old and rarely used in everyday modern speech, but you may encounter it in older literature, poetry, or historical texts, so it is worth knowing.

In this sense, a jade is a horse that is old, exhausted, worn down, and no longer capable of working well — a tired, broken-down animal that has been overworked. It is not an affectionate term; it implies a horse that is past its prime and of little value.

This meaning extended, by metaphor, to describe a person (historically, a woman) who was considered disreputable or ill-tempered — but this usage is now considered offensive and archaic. You are unlikely to need to use it; you only need to recognise it if you come across it in old texts.

It is worth briefly knowing the adjective jaded, because it grows directly from the second noun meaning above (the exhausted horse). If you are jaded, you are:

  • Worn out, bored, and unimpressed because you have had too much of something.
  • No longer able to feel excitement, pleasure, or enthusiasm about something that used to be stimulating.

For example: a food critic who eats at the finest restaurants every day might become jaded — nothing excites their palate anymore. A traveller who has seen every major city in the world might feel jaded about yet another famous landmark.

The image is of being so overexposed to something good that it has lost all its shine — like a horse ridden so hard it collapses.

Primary meaningA beautiful, hard, semi-precious stone, most famously green, deeply important in Chinese and other cultures. Comes in two types: jadeite (rarer, more vivid) and nephrite (more common, subtler). Used in jewellery, carvings, and ornamental objects.
Secondary meaning (archaic)A worn-out, useless old horse. Found in old literature.
